summary: Specifies the Diameter base protocol, a framework for Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) used in network access and IP mobility, including roaming. It defines the message format, transport, error reporting, accounting, and security services shared by Diameter applications. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Diameter is like a door guard who checks who you are, decides what you may do, and keeps a count of what you used. This memo sets the common rules guards follow.

questions: what is an avp in diameter
subtitle: The common rulebook for Authentication, Authorization and Accounting between network devices, servers and the agents in between.

tldr.problem: Networks need one dependable way to decide who may use a service, what they may do and how much they used, including when the user is roaming through another operator. RADIUS left failover, transport security and server-initiated messages undefined or optional.
tldr.mechanism: Diameter is a peer-to-peer protocol over reliable transport (TCP or SCTP) in which every message is a header plus a list of Attribute-Value Pairs. The base protocol defines peer setup, routing through relay, proxy, redirect and translation agents, error reporting, session handling and accounting. Applications then add their own commands and AVPs.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6733 obsoletes RFC 3588 and RFC 5719 and is backward compatible with RFC 3588. It was itself later updated by RFC 7075 and RFC 8553. All new Diameter implementations must support it.

today: RFC 6733 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3588 and RFC 5719, and it has since been updated by RFC 7075 and RFC 8553. It is the base specification that Diameter applications build on, and its abstract says it must be supported by all new Diameter implementations.

sections.title: Why Diameter Exists
sections.content:
RFC 6733 specifies the Diameter base protocol, an Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA) framework for uses such as network access and IP mobility, in both local and roaming situations. It defines the message format, transport, error reporting, accounting and security services shared by every Diameter application.

The introduction lists what earlier AAA protocols such as RADIUS lacked. RADIUS does not define failover, requires per-packet security only for responses, runs over UDP without defined retransmission, has no explicit agent behavior, makes server-initiated messages optional, and has no error messages or capability negotiation. Diameter answers each: application-layer acknowledgements with failover algorithms, TLS/TCP and DTLS/SCTP security, reliable transport (TCP and SCTP), explicitly defined agents, mandatory server-initiated messages, error handling, capability negotiation and DNS-based peer discovery.

The base protocol can be used by itself for accounting. For authentication and authorization it is always extended by a Diameter application, such as the Mobile IPv4 application (RFC 4004) or the network access application (RFC 4005). Extension works by adding new commands or AVPs, and the RFC sets rules for when a new Command Code or a whole new application is required.

Any node can initiate a request, which is why the RFC calls Diameter a peer-to-peer protocol. A client is a device at the network edge that enforces access control, a server authenticates and/or authorizes the user, and an agent is a node that does neither locally.
sections.eli5: Older door guards could not tell each other when they were sick, and they shouted instead of sending safe notes. Diameter gives them a proper, reliable way to talk and to swap places when one of them is away.

sections.title: Peers, Agents and Sessions
sections.content:
Diameter separates a connection from a session. A connection is a transport-level link between two peers. A session is an application-layer relationship between a client and a server, identified by a Session-Id AVP. Messages for many sessions are multiplexed over one connection, and there is no relationship between the two.

Between client and server may sit four kinds of agent:

  • Relay agents route requests using the Destination-Realm AVP and the routing table. They change only routing information, must advertise the Relay Application Id and should not keep session state, though they must keep transaction state.
  • Proxy agents also route, but may modify messages to enforce policy such as admission control, so they advertise only the applications they support.
  • Redirect agents do not forward anything. They return the contact details of the right server so the sender can talk to it directly.
  • Translation agents convert between protocols, for example RADIUS and Diameter, and must be session stateful.

Each node keeps a peer table (the directly reachable peers) and a routing table keyed first by realm name and second by Application Id. A route entry has a local action of LOCAL, RELAY, PROXY or REDIRECT, and the table may include a default entry.

Path authorization matters too. Before bringing up a connection a peer must check that the other side is authorized to act in its role, and a home server must inspect the Route-Record AVPs to confirm that the request did not traverse an unacceptable realm. If it did, it sends DIAMETER_AUTHORIZATION_REJECTED.
sections.eli5: A client is a visitor at the front desk, the server is the office that knows them, and the agents are mail rooms between the two. Some mail rooms just pass letters on, some stamp their own rules on them, and one only tells you which office to go to.

sections.title: The Diameter Header
sections.content:
Every Diameter message begins with a fixed header: Version (must be 1), a three-octet Message Length that covers the header and the padded AVPs, an eight-bit Command Flags field, a three-octet Command Code, a four-octet Application-ID, a Hop-by-Hop Identifier and an End-to-End Identifier, followed by the AVPs.

The command flags are R (request, otherwise answer), P (the message may be proxied, relayed or redirected), E (the message carries a protocol error) and T (a possibly retransmitted request, set after a failover). The remaining four bits are reserved and must be zero.

The two identifiers do different jobs. The Hop-by-Hop Identifier matches answers to requests on one connection, and an agent replaces it with a locally unique value when forwarding and restores it on the way back. The End-to-End Identifier detects duplicates, must not be changed by any agent, and must stay locally unique for at least 4 minutes, even across reboots. Together with Origin-Host it identifies a duplicate request.

A request and its answer share one Command Code and differ only in the R bit. Each command is specified in a Command Code Format (CCF), an ABNF-based grammar that marks AVPs as fixed, required { } or optional [ ], and usually allows any further optional AVP at the end to leave room for extension.
sections.eli5: The header is the label on an envelope: what kind of message it is, whether it is a question or an answer, which service it is for, and two tracking numbers so replies find their way home.

sections.title: Attribute-Value Pairs
sections.content:
All data in Diameter travels as Attribute-Value Pairs (AVPs). An AVP has an AVP Code, a flags byte, a three-octet AVP Length, an optional four-octet Vendor-ID and the data. Codes 1 to 255 are reserved for reuse of RADIUS attributes, and codes from 256 up are Diameter's and allocated by IANA. Values are padded with zero bytes to a 32-bit boundary, and the padding is not counted in the AVP Length.

The flags that matter are V (a Vendor-ID follows, so the code lives in that vendor's own space) and M, the Mandatory bit. If a receiver gets an AVP with M set that it does not understand, it must return an error. An AVP with M cleared is informational and may simply be ignored. The P bit is reserved for future end-to-end security; the RFC says no such mechanism is specified, so it should be 0.

Base data types include OctetString, Integer32, Integer64, Unsigned32 and Unsigned64, with common derived types such as DiameterIdentity. A Grouped AVP carries a sequence of other AVPs in its data and may nest, and each Grouped AVP needs its own ABNF-style grammar.
sections.eli5: An AVP is a labeled box. The label says what is inside, a little switch says whether the receiver must understand it, and the box is padded so every box ends at a neat boundary.

sections.title: Peer Connections and Capabilities
sections.content:
Diameter runs over TCP or SCTP on port 3868, and clients must support at least one of those two, while agents and servers should support both. Connections are meant to be secured with TLS (over TCP) or DTLS (over SCTP). A node should try TLS first, then DTLS, then TCP and finally SCTP, and falls back to the older unprotected approach only for backward compatibility. If no connection exists, a node retries periodically, driven by the Tc timer whose recommended value is 30 seconds.

Peers can be found by static configuration or through DNS. The suggested search order is the static list, then a NAPTR query using the service tag aaa with tags such as diameter.tcp and diameter.sctp, then direct SRV queries such as _diameter._tcp.realm. Even a securely discovered peer must still be checked for authorization to act as a Diameter server, because a valid certificate does not prove that.

Once connected, each side sends a Capabilities-Exchange-Request (CER, Command Code 257) and answers with a CEA. These carry identity, IP addresses, vendor and product details and the supported Application Ids. The receiver computes the applications in common and, if there are none, answers DIAMETER_NO_COMMON_APPLICATION. A node that advertises the Relay Application Id is treated as supporting everything.

Other base messages manage the link. Device-Watchdog (DWR/DWA, 280) detects dead connections, and Disconnect-Peer (DPR/DPA, 282) tells a peer why a node is closing the connection (REBOOTING, BUSY or DO_NOT_WANT_TO_TALK_TO_YOU). When a transport failure is detected, pending requests are resent to an alternate peer with the T flag set (failover), and traffic returns once the connection is rebuilt (failback). Duplicates are caught with the End-to-End Identifier and Origin-Host.

All of this is driven by a mandatory peer state machine. Its stable states are Closed, I-Open (initiator side) and R-Open (responder side). If two nodes connect to each other at the same moment, an election compares the two Origin-Host values as octet strings, and the loser's connection is closed.
sections.eli5: Before two servers chat, they shake hands and show each other a list of the jobs they can do. They also keep poking each other to check the line is alive, and say goodbye politely when one needs to leave.

sections.title: Routing and Message Processing
sections.content:
A request is routed by its Destination-Realm AVP and the Application Id in its header. The realm can be taken from the realm part of the user's NAI in the User-Name AVP. Destination-Host is added only when the destination is fixed, for instance for authentication that spans several round trips. Messages that cannot be forwarded, like a CER, carry neither.

An originator sets the R bit, a locally unique End-to-End Identifier, and the Origin-Host and Origin-Realm AVPs. A relay or proxy that forwards a request must append a Route-Record AVP naming the peer it came from, save and replace the Hop-by-Hop Identifier, and check for loops. If it finds its own identity in a Route-Record, it answers DIAMETER_LOOP_DETECTED. Agents also avoid candidate routes whose peer already appears in a Route-Record.

A redirect agent answers with the E bit set, the result DIAMETER_REDIRECT_INDICATION and one Redirect-Host AVP per candidate server. The Redirect-Host-Usage AVP can tell the receiver to cache the redirect (for example ALL_SESSION or ALL_REALM), and Redirect-Max-Cache-Time sets how long. When cached routes conflict, a precedence rule applies, starting with ALL_SESSION.

Answers reuse the request's Hop-by-Hop and End-to-End identifiers and the Session-Id, carry the answering host's Origin-Host, and omit Destination-Host and Destination-Realm. A relay must not alter a failure Result-Code it forwards.
sections.eli5: Each message has a destination written on it, and every mail room adds its name to a list as it passes the message along. If a mail room sees its own name already on the list, it stops, because the message is going in circles.

sections.title: Error Reporting
sections.content:
Diameter distinguishes protocol errors, which occur at the base level and may need attention at each hop (such as a routing failure), from application errors, which concern a function of a particular application (such as a missing AVP). Protocol errors travel in answers with the E bit set. Application errors are returned to the originator without special handling by agents.

The Result-Code AVP is mandatory in IETF-defined answers, and its class is the thousands digit: 1xxx informational, 2xxx success, 3xxx protocol errors, 4xxx transient failures and 5xxx permanent failures. An unrecognized class must be treated as a permanent failure. If a node detects several errors it reports only the first.

Some errors need extra detail. An unrecognized mandatory AVP gives DIAMETER_AVP_UNSUPPORTED, a bad value gives DIAMETER_INVALID_AVP_VALUE, and a missing required AVP gives DIAMETER_MISSING_AVP. In each case the Failed-AVP AVP carries the offending AVP, or a created one showing what was expected. If the node setting an error is not the one named in Origin-Host, it adds an Error-Reporting-Host AVP.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong, the answer carries a number from a code book. The first digit says what kind of trouble it is: need more steps, all fine, a delivery problem, try again later, or do not bother trying again.

sections.title: User Sessions
sections.content:
The first request for a user carries a Session-Id, and every later message about that session reuses it. A Session-Id must begin with the sender's DiameterIdentity, followed by ;-separated parts, and it must be globally and eternally unique. A recommended layout uses two decimal 32-bit halves of an increasing 64-bit counter.

The base protocol defines no authorization request of its own, because those belong to applications. It does define the messages that manage a session:

  • Re-Auth-Request / Answer (RAR/RAA, 258): a server asks the access device to re-authenticate or re-authorize the user, for example to confirm a prepaid user is still active.
  • Session-Termination-Request / Answer (STR/STA, 275): the access device tells the server the session is over so state can be freed. An STR is required whenever a session ends for any reason, and also for a session that was authorized but never started.
  • Abort-Session-Request / Answer (ASR/ASA, 274): a server asks the access device to stop service, for example for lack of credit. The device may decline but must answer.

A server limits a session with the Authorization-Lifetime and Auth-Grace-Period AVPs. A client that does not plan to send re-authorization or termination messages can hint Auth-Session-State as NO_STATE_MAINTAINED, and the server may then keep no state. The RFC gives four authorization state machines (stateful and stateless, client and server) that all implementations must observe. They move through Idle, Pending, Open and Discon states.
sections.eli5: A session is like a library visit with a numbered ticket. The server can ask you to show your card again, ask you to leave, or you can tell the desk you are done so they can clear your seat.

sections.title: Accounting
sections.content:
Diameter accounting is a server directed model. The server tells the device generating the data how and how quickly to report, mainly through the Acct-Interim-Interval AVP (produce records during the session) and the Accounting-Realtime-Required AVP (what to do when delivery is delayed or fails). Real-time transfer is required, and batch accounting is not supported at the Diameter layer.

A client sends an Accounting-Request (ACR, Command Code 271) and the server confirms with an Accounting-Answer (ACA). The Accounting-Record-Type AVP says what kind of record it is: EVENT_RECORD (a one-time event), or START_RECORD, INTERIM_RECORD and STOP_RECORD for a service of measurable length. Every record includes a Session-Id. Without interim accounting, two records are generated per session, one start and one stop.

Applications may use a split accounting service, where accounting messages carry the base accounting Application Id and may go to central accounting servers, or a coupled one, where they carry the application's own Id. For fault resilience, clients must fail over, may keep records in non-volatile memory until acknowledged, and agents or off-line systems must detect duplicate records by the Session-Id and Accounting-Record-Number pair.
sections.eli5: Accounting is the meter on the wall. It writes down when you started, can check in now and then while you are using things, and writes a final number when you stop, and it keeps the notes safe until the office says it got them.

sections.title: Security and Changes from RFC 3588
sections.content:
Diameter base messages should be secured with TLS or DTLS/SCTP, and IPsec may also be used. All base implementations must support TLS/TCP and DTLS/SCTP, and Diameter must not be used without one of TLS, DTLS or IPsec. Securing the connection before any CER/CEA exchange protects the capabilities information. Nodes using TLS must mutually authenticate, and the RFC lists the cipher suites that must or should be supported.

The RFC also warns that trust configuration is essential in a peer-to-peer protocol. Root certificate authorities for Diameter are likely to differ from those trusted for web browsing, and the RFC notes that at the time of writing no Diameter server certificate authorities existed. Security-sensitive AVPs, such as User-Name, Session-Id and the accounting AVPs, may only be sent over mutually authenticated TLS or IPsec. They must not pass through intermediaries without end-to-end security or a locally trusted configuration, and the RFC states that no end-to-end mechanism is specified.

Compared with RFC 3588, this document is fully backward compatible but deprecates negotiating TLS via the Inband-Security AVP in favor of a well-known secured port (the older method is kept for compatibility), deprecates CER/CEA in the open state (re-introduced in RFC 6737), and deprecates the End-to-End security framework. It also relaxes Command Code allocation for vendors, clarifies Application Id usage and routing, and narrows peer discovery to widely used schemes.
sections.eli5: The messages carry private information, so they must travel in a locked bag and both sides must show ID. The newer rules make the locked bag the normal way instead of an optional extra.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Must be set to 1 for Diameter Version 1.

fields.name: Message Length
fields.desc: Length of the whole message including the header and padded AVPs; always a multiple of 4.

fields.name: Command Flags
fields.desc: R, P, E, T and four reserved bits.

fields.name: Command Code
fields.desc: Identifies the command; the 24-bit space is managed by IANA.

fields.name: Application-ID
fields.desc: The application the message applies to.

fields.name: Hop-by-Hop Identifier
fields.desc: Matches answers to requests on one connection.

fields.name: End-to-End Identifier
fields.desc: Detects duplicate messages; never changed by agents.

fields.name: AVP Code
fields.desc: With the Vendor-ID, identifies the attribute uniquely.

fields.name: V M P r r r r r
fields.desc: Vendor-specific, Mandatory and reserved-for-security bits, then five reserved bits.

fields.name: AVP Length
fields.desc: Octets in the AVP, excluding padding.

fields.name: Vendor-ID (optional)
fields.desc: Present only when the V bit is set.
